gotcha-py.main.py:
import asyncio

log = []


async def heartbeat():
    for i in range(1, 4):
        log.append(f"tick {i}")
        await asyncio.sleep(0)  # let the event loop run something else


async def main():
    hb = asyncio.create_task(heartbeat())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # let the heartbeat start

    # CPU-bound work, called straight from a coroutine
    total = sum(n % 7 for n in range(1_000_000))
    log.append(f"sum done, total {total}")

    await hb
    print("\n".join(log))


asyncio.run(main())

langs.offload.py:
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor


def work() -> int:
    return sum(n % 7 for n in range(1_000_000))


async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        print("process pool:", await loop.run_in_executor(pool, work))
    print("to_thread:", await asyncio.to_thread(work))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

gotcha.title: `par_iter` inside an `async fn`
gotcha.looks_fine: A parallel loop is a function call that returns the right answer, and a loop inside an async function is ordinary code in most languages.
gotcha.rust_sees: `par_iter().sum()` is a blocking call: rayon does the work on its own threads, but the call does not return until they finish, and the thread that made the call waits. In an `async fn` that thread belongs to the runtime. Here the runtime has one thread, so the heartbeat task gets no turn between "tick 1" and the end of the sum. On the default multi-thread runtime the same call would hold one worker thread instead (the Tokio docs describe the swapping as happening on each thread); this page runs only the one-thread case.
gotcha.why: Tokio can switch tasks only at an `.await`; its docs say code that spends a long time without reaching one "will prevent other tasks from running". The order above does not depend on how long the sum takes, only on there being no `.await` in it. Hand the work to rayon with `rayon::spawn` and wait on a `tokio::sync::oneshot` channel instead: the task awaits, so the runtime thread is free, and the heartbeat ticks while the job waits. The rayon job in the fix waits on a std channel until the heartbeat has ticked three times; that gate fixes the order, and without it the order would depend on timing.

python.says: `asyncio` has the same rule: the `sum` has no `await`, so the event loop cannot run the heartbeat until it returns. The log has the same order as the Rust one, so there is no difference to show for Python: it is the same trap.
